source.title: RoboMonkey: Scaling Test-Time Sampling and Verification for Vision-Language-Action Models
source.authors: Jacky Kwok; Christopher Agia; Rohan Sinha; Matt Foutter; Shulu Li; Ion Stoica; Azalia Mirhoseini; Marco Pavone

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to test-time action sampling for vision-language-action policies in robotics; it measures action error against sample count, rather than language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or training compute.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are action-error curves versus test-time sample count. Other reported task-success, latency, verifier-training, and baseline-comparison results are not rows unless they directly measure a scaling result bearing on a claim version. The paper also cites language-model scaling work, but cited results are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study's scaling result is inference-time best-of-k action error versus number of samples, scored by an oracle verifier, in robot VLA policies. That is not loss falling with parameters, tokens or training compute, nor any training regime that V5 names. It measures a different construct: an order-statistics effect of selecting among more candidates. The paper only cites training-compute scaling for VLAs without testing it. The verifier dataset-size result reports fine-tuning data versus closed-loop task success, described as 'nearly log-linear', with no power-law loss fit. So no version is tested, and both findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim an approximate ('exponentiated') power law between action error and sample count, but only under an oracle verifier. They also claim that scaling synthetic verifier-training data consistently improves success, and that RoboMonkey gives +25% on real-world out-of-distribution tasks, +9% on in-distribution SIMPLER tasks, and +7% on LIBERO-Long when fine-tuned.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures robot action error against test-time candidate count, rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or training compute; it uses oracle or learned action verification.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares random sampling, repeated policy sampling, and Gaussian perturbation; Gaussian perturbation is described as nearly matching policy sampling while being more computationally efficient. The reported curves and model-specific reductions vary by VLA.

fits_no_version.finding: With an oracle verifier, the minimum action RMSE among k sampled actions falls approximately as a power law in k (log e ≈ log a + b log k). This holds across CogACT, Octo, OpenVLA and SpatialVLA and across sampling methods; for OpenVLA, error falls 59.3% at 10,000 samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time repeated-sampling scaling: oracle best-of-k error falls as a power law in sample count across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Closed-loop task success of a policy guided by the learned verifier rises roughly log-linearly with the size of the synthetic preference dataset used to fine-tune the verifier (average 37.5% to 46.3%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning data scale for reward models or verifiers predicts downstream task success roughly log-linearly.

record.problems: The power-law curves are primarily presented in figures, and the text gives few model-specific curve values. The scaling analysis uses 1,000 Bridge V2 tuples; uncertainty for the action-error scaling results is not stated. The study measures robotics action error, not held-out language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: Task-success comparisons, latency measurements, and verifier-quality ablations are not included because they do not directly report the tested action-error-versus-test-time-sample-count relation. The separate synthetic-dataset-size success-rate results are retained as R11–R12 under versions none because they concern verifier training-data scale rather than the stated versions.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small training runs.
All: no shape ablations at fixed parameter count.
All: no training-regime or modality loss scaling. The test-time best-of-k curves are a different construct.
All: no downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss.
All: no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 links are rejected because V5 concerns training regimes and modalities for the loss power law, whereas this is test-time best-of-k selection. Power-law fit parameters (a, b) are not reported numerically, and no uncertainty is given for the oracle curves; error bars appear only in the Appendix F ablation. R7–R10 are the study's own method against baselines and should be marked as such.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, and training compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation under a fixed training-compute budget.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests action error versus test-time sampling in robotics VLAs, not held-out pretraining loss; does not test image/video models, repeated training data, fine-tuning, or transfer as such.
Does not test downstream-task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Does not vary fitting choices or test whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with setup.

rows.subject: OpenVLA
rows.operation_detail: Increase the number of candidate actions generated using Gaussian perturbation; select the candidate with an oracle verifier for the scaling analysis.

conditions.value: Bridge V2 auxiliary dataset; 1,000 sampled tuples

rows.measure: Normalized RMSE of selected action against ground-truth action
rows.baseline: single-attempt OpenVLA; exact RMSE not stated
rows.value: RMSE decreases by 59.3% when sampling 10,000 actions
rows.note: The paper describes an approximate power-law relationship between action error and sample count; the reported 59.3% decrease is for OpenVLA.
rows.check: Measures oracle best-of-k action error versus test-time sample count, not loss versus training scale or regime. Not V5. Baseline single-attempt RMSE not given numerically.

rows.check: Same inference-time construct as R1, not V5. Figure-only value; per-model fit parameters not stated.
